title: DFS on New York (SoHo) ⚡
description: Visualizing DFS pathfinding on New York (SoHo)
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps—what happens when DFS explores city intersections ⚡?

In this reel, each street intersection is a node and each street segment is an edge (a graph). DFS follows the “go as deep as possible” rule using a stack/recursion pattern: it marks a node visited, then keeps choosing the next neighbor until it can’t, then backtracks.

Key DFS behaviors you’ll see on the map:
• Visit order depends on neighbor ordering (your “direction priority”)
• DFS finds *a* path, not necessarily the shortest (unlike BFS)
• Backtracking creates the distinctive “deep dive → rewind → dive again” pattern

Takeaway: DFS is great for reachability, cycle detection, and exploring connected components—but for shortest paths on unweighted graphs, BFS is the usual go-to.

Debate question: If we change the neighbor ordering (left-first vs right-first), should the “best-looking” city route be considered better—even if it’s longer?
